topic.title: Why 'The Simpsons predicted it' spreads
topic.claim: We share 'The Simpsons predicted it' because a coincidence with a script feels safer than a world where things just happen.
topic.behaviour: A cartoon clip resurfaces on the same day as a real outage. People send it around as proof that someone knew in advance.
topic.mechanism: A pattern is easier to bear than chaos, and a prediction clip is easy to post. The people who post it get reach without having to check anything.
topic.group: Heavy Instagram and X users who forward clips to friends
topic.moment: A friend sends you a clip with 'bro, look at the date' and nothing else.

turn.believed: The clip is spooky because it matches the news.
turn.actually: It matches because we went looking for the match. The details that don't fit never get posted.

topic.feeling: a bit foolish for almost believing it
topic.villain: a feed that rewards the spookiest version of a coincidence
topic.because: A spooky post earns shares, and shares are the point. Checking would kill the post.

proof.fact: A clip from the 2023 Simpsons episode 'It's A Blunderful Life' shows an older Lisa writing about a blackout in her diary, dated November 17. Skeptics noted that Lisa's diary never mentions 2026.

topic.payoff: A prediction that needs three real events and one missing year to work is not a prediction.
topic.send_to: The friend who forwards every 'they knew' clip
real_details: It resurfaced alongside a Microsoft outage and a scheduled US emergency alert test on the same date
topic.news_peg: The Simpsons blackout clip resurfaced on 17 November 2026
topic.why_now: The clip went viral on 17 November and the pattern repeats with every big news day.

score.why: The 'bro, look at the date' forward: we hunt for the match and never post what doesn't fit. It adds a funny mood and an argument, and the sourced detail is only light colour.
